idiom_name: iterator interface + concrete cursor + aggregate creation operation (or the language's iteration protocol)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the aggregate a creation operation (createIterator()/iterator()/makeIterator()/All()) that returns the abstract iterator; keep the cursor state inside the iterator object, never on the aggregate; and let clients loop through hasNext()/next() or the local equivalent (a begin/end pair, a {value, done} result object, an Option-returning next(), or a callback/yield). Decide up front whether each call hands out a fresh iterator (replayable collection) or a single-use cursor (streaming source), and make modification during traversal either fail-fast or explicitly documented. Where the language supplies an iteration protocol, generator syntax, or lazy pipeline, implement that instead of the two-class structural pattern.
code_sketch:
it = aggregate.iterator()
while it.has_next():
    element = it.next()
    use(element)
# or, where the language has a protocol/generator:
# for element in aggregate: use(element)
# or, with a generator:
# def gen(aggregate):
#     for e in aggregate._items:
#         yield e
pitfalls: Storing the cursor on the aggregate so that only one traversal can exist at a time.
Handing out iterators that expose or mutate the aggregate's internals (public fields, friend access, raw node pointers).
Leaving behaviour undefined when the aggregate changes mid-traversal; clients will end up depending on whatever accidentally happens.
Returning an exhausted cursor or spent generator where callers expect a replayable collection.
Implementing a custom cursor in a language that already has a rich iteration protocol.
Iterator exhaustion: passing an already-consumed iterator to a second consumer silently yields nothing — the second for-loop or list() call gets zero items with no error.
hasNext() that advances the cursor as a side effect; calling it twice skips an element.
Iterator whose next() raises a checked exception on termination instead of signalling done — callers must handle it as a special case rather than a clean loop end.
Missing __iter__ (Python) or Symbol.iterator (JS) on a custom iterator class, causing for/in loops to throw TypeError at runtime instead of working.
for...in on a custom iterable in JavaScript iterates over property keys, not values — must use for...of.
